newsitem.title: USA: Slow Miami aircargo trade seeks Mother's Day boost.
newsitem.headline: Slow Miami aircargo trade seeks Mother's Day boost.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Miami International Airport (MIA) are little changed, as air cargo executives and forwarders prepare for the Mother's Day flower rush and wonder about the effect of new trade sanctions imposed by Brazil, a Reuters survey shows.
Carriers to European destinations contine to drop fuel surcharges and freight forwarders expect to see the same to Latin America.
"Fuel surcharges have not dropped yet to Latin America, but we are expecting to see that shortly," one forwarder said.
There may also be some softening and more volatility in rates to London. Laker Airways is now flying to and from Florida, adding capacity to the market.
Rates to London traditionally become weaker and more volatile in the summer with the flood of holiday charters to Florida, especially Orlando.
Rates to London from MIA dropped only five U.S. cents to $1.15 per kg since the last Reuters ex-Miami Air Cargo Market Report in March.
"We see the rates (to London) dropping," said one forwarder, "but some of these operators do not have the experience of say a British Airways. Still, they push the rates down."
The airfreight community is bracing for a healthy Mother's Day flower lift, which starts at the end of April and ends a few days before the Mother's Day holiday on May 11.

"We will have a satisfactory Mother's Day this year. It may be too early to tell, but it doesn't look like it is going to be one of those gangbuster years," the chief executive of one all-cargo airline that serves Latin America said.
"We expect a good Mother's Day," said Barbara Montes, sales and marketing manager for CFX Inc, a big Miami-based importer and grower of cut flowers.
But forwarders fear they won't be seeing the traditional rate slashing southbound on the flower growing routes.
"They are right. They won't be getting them from us," an airline executive said.
In past years, forwarders have benefited from bargain basement rates southbound from Miami around the holiday.
Extra flights are added to handle the huge volumes of northbound flower shipments and the market briefly is flooded with excess capacity to Colombia and other flower growing countries.
But for Valentine's Day this year, carriers stood firm and dropped southbound rates only slightly and forwarders say they expect Mother's Day to be the same.
"We will be able to spot (rate)," said one forwarder, "but we won't see those 18 cent rates again."
Currently rates to Bogota from MIA are around 65 cents per kg, but have dropped to as little as 10 cents per kg during peak flower airlifts in years past.
On an average day, Miami International Airport receives about 30,000 boxes of flowers, but around Mother's Day that more than doubles to about 70,000 boxes per day, according to MIA statistics.
Mother's Day surpasses Valentine's Day in volume of flowers imported, but Valentine's Day represents a higher dollar volume, CFX's Montes said.

Long-stemmed red roses, the preferred Valentine flower, are costlier than the wide variety of flowers given to mothers, Montes said. Mothers get mostly carnations and chrysanthemums and other less expensive blooms, Montes noted.
Other than flowers, the perishable season in Latin America is easing off, as spring comes to North America and it can produce its own fruits and vegetables.
The freight forwarding community is cheering the recently initiated weekly Boeing 747 freighter service by China Airlines.
The service, which started in mid-March, "is the best news right now," said one forwarder.
It is the first direct service from Miami to the Far East and links up the two important markets of Latin America and Asia, the forwarders said.
Rates from Miami to Asia are about $2.25 to $2.50 per kg, depending on the destination, forwarders said.
Air cargo executives and forwarders are keeping a wary eye on Brazil, which has put in place some import restrictions.
Effective April 1, Brazil instituted "a non-tariff barrier to trade", Charles Jainarain, executive director of the Summit of the Americas Centre at Florida Intenational University, Miami.
"They are requiring imports of consumer goods to be paid for by cash," Jainarain said. "This will depress the level of imports of consumer goods such as cell phones, VCRs, TVs etc.," he added.
"They have not yet formulated exactly what they are doing, but it will definitely impact air cargo," Bill Spohrer, president of Challenge Air Cargo, the Miami-based all-cargo carrier, said.
"This is unfortunate for Florida," Jainarain said.

Indeed, Brazil is MIA's biggest trading partner. Brazil accounted for $274 million of air trade through Miami International Airport in 1995, the most recent statistics available from the Dade County Aviation Department show.
